episode.subject: harbor seal with fish and gulls
episode.title: I showed them twice
episode.body:
Every time I came up, they were waiting. I took the fish deeper. Came up farther away. They found me before I had swallowed.

When it was gone, I stayed at the surface with my mouth closed.

One landed beside me. Then another.

I opened my mouth to show them.

They stayed. I stopped showing them.

heldDrafts.fictionBoundary: Primary observer reports repeated submerging and surfacing to bite fish while gulls sought pieces. Depth change, evasion, swallowing completion, landing order, showing empty mouth and acceptance of company are fictional. Images show the earlier fish-in-mouth phase; do not label the mouth empty in alt text.
heldDrafts.continuity: Prospective adult incident after current two episodes. Source Whidbey Island illustrates species, not a journey from Kenai Fjords. No sex, subspecies or maternal role asserted.
heldDrafts.authorReview: Concrete draft explores unwanted company becoming tolerable when the assumed reason for it disappears. It avoids a stolen-meal payoff, but may overstate gull persistence after food is gone. That is a fictional moment rather than a biology claim. Image failure remains decisive: no runtime proposal until a sharper exact image earns the group scene.

3 Humpback Whales, very close to shore, rolling around in the kelp bed in Monterey Bay, CA.

My favorite Humpback Whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=41566&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1
Spy-hopping with Barnacles, in Monterey Bay: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/95007656

Humpback Whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) is a large marine mammal in the Baleen Whales (Mysticeti) Parvorder. Baleen Whales feed on plankton which they strain from seawater.
Conservation Status: Vulnerable (N3) in United States (NatureServe)
Conservation Status: Species of Special Concern in Canada (Canadian Species at Risk Act)

The Humpback Whale is a baleen whale that feeds on plankton which it strains from seawater. Adults range in length from 12–16 m (39–52 ft) and weigh about 36,000 kg (79,000 lb). The humpback has a distinctive body shape, with long, mostly white pectoral fins and a head that is often covered with barnacles. It is known for breaching, spy hopping, lunge feeding and other distinctive surface behaviors. Males produce a complex song, lasting 10 to 20 minutes, which they repeat for hours. If only we could understand what they are trying to tell us. Protect our oceans, for one thing!
Found in oceans and seas around the world, Humpback Whales typically migrate up to 16,000 km (9,900 mi) each year. They feed in polar waters and migrate to tropical or subtropical waters to breed and give birth. Their diet consists mostly of krill and small fish. Unique among large whales, humpbacks sometime hunt in groups using bubbles to concentrate and catch prey. They are promiscuous breeders, with both sexes having multiple partners. Orcas are the main natural predators of humpback whales.
Like other large whales, the humpback has been a target for the whaling industry. Humans once hunted the species to the brink of extinction; its population fell to around 5,000 by the 1960s. Japan and some indigenous groups continue to hunt several species of whale, despite the 1982 ban on whaling by the International Whaling Commission. Many countries have realized that whale watching/tourism is more profitable. While numbers have partially recovered to some 135,000 animals worldwide, limited hunting, entanglement in fishing gear, collisions with ships, and noise pollution continue to affect the species.

Whale Barnacles: https://scienceline.org/2010/03/how-do-barnacles-attach-to-whales/

Link to Humpback Whale Barnacle (Coronula diadema) observation:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/95008190

Whale Barnacles: From: https://marinesanctuary.org/sanctuary/monterey-bay/ website:
"Specific species of Barnacles generally live of specific species of whales, a likely result of geographic location of each. For example, the barnacle Coronula diaderma has only been recorded living on humpback whales and Cryptolepas rhachianecti live only on gray whales."

Cetaceans (Infraorder Cetacea) are marine mammals that include whales, dolphins, and porpoises. Key characteristics are their fully aquatic lifestyle, streamlined body shape, often large size and exclusively carnivorous diet. They propel themselves through the water with powerful up-and-down movement of their tail which ends in a paddle-like fluke, using their flipper-shaped forelimbs to maneuver.
Cetaceans are primarily marine mammals, but a few species are adapted to freshwater environments.
Most cetaceans—including whales, dolphins, and porpoises—live in marine habitats, ranging from coastal zones to deep ocean basins. However, some species are exclusively or partially freshwater dwellers, particularly river dolphins.

Odd‑toed Ungulates (Perissodactyla order) include animals that place their weight on one or three toes. Zebras are one example; they live across eastern and southern Africa in grasslands, savannas, and open woodlands. Black rhinoceroses are another example, found in eastern and southern Africa in scrublands and savannas. Domestic Horse (Equus caballus) is another example.

Irene's Even-toed Ungulates and Cetaceans (Order Artiodactyla) observations on INaturalist, worldwide: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?verifiable=any&taxon_id=152870&preferred_place_id=917&user_id=aparrot1

Even‑toed Ungulates (Order Artiodactyla) place their weight on two toes. Giraffes are one example; they live across sub‑Saharan Africa in savannas and open woodlands. White‑tailed deer are another example, found throughout North America in forests, grasslands, and suburban areas. Wild boars also belong to this group and are native to Europe and Asia but now occur widely in North America and many other regions. Bighorn Sheep (Ovis canadensis) is another terrestrial example; the aquatic Humpback Whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) is another Even‑toed Ungulates example.

Placental mammals are the group of terrestrial and aquatic animals whose babies develop inside the mother for a long time because they have a true placenta, which is an organ that passes food and oxygen from the mother to the embryo. This long internal development means the young are born much more fully formed than marsupials, whose babies are born very early and finish growing in a pouch, or monotremes, which lay eggs. A familiar marsupial example is the Virginia Opossum, and a common monotreme example is the Platypus.
Placental mammals also lack epipubic bones, which are stiff rods in the belly region found in marsupials and monotremes. Losing those bones lets the abdomen expand during pregnancy. Their ankle has a particular locking shape called a mortise joint, which helps with stable walking and running. They usually have a strong connection between the left and right halves of the brain called the corpus callosum, which is reduced or missing in other mammal groups. And unlike monotremes, they do not have a cloaca, which is a single opening for waste and reproduction; instead, the openings are separate.

and glossary: https://animaldiversity.org/glossary/

Placental mammals also lack epipubic bones, which are stiff rods in the belly region found in marsupials and monotremes. Losing those bones lets the abdomen expand during pregnancy. Their ankle has a particular locking shape called a mortise joint, which helps with stable walking and running. They usually have a strong connection between the left and right halves of the brain called the corpus callosum, which is reduced or missing in other mammal groups. And unlike monotremes, they do not have a cloaca, which is a single opening for waste and reproduction; instead, the openings are separate.
